rationale: The book establishes its distinguishing core for the cited texts and garment imagery: righteousness is enacted obedience, not merely an inward quality or forensic verdict. Deuteronomy 6:25 directly calls observing the commandments “our righteousness”; Psalm 119:172 identifies the commandments with righteousness; 1 John 3:7 makes doing righteousness constitutive of being righteous; and Revelation 19:8 explicitly interprets the wedding linen as the saints’ righteous acts. The strongest forensic counter-reading explains the garment’s being given, cleansing by blood, and “put on Christ” language well, but it cannot account as naturally for Revelation’s explicit identification of the linen with deeds. Nevertheless, the evidence does not establish the book’s broader tendency to treat this as a uniform definition in every biblical context, nor every link in its extended symbolic construction. Pauline texts about righteousness counted apart from works and passages describing God’s own righteousness require lexical and contextual distinctions that this chapter does not adequately address.
book_core_identification: In the cited ethical and garment contexts, righteousness denotes obedience performed—the doing of God’s commands—and the righteous garment is made up of such righteous acts rather than being only a forensic status.
book_secondary_elaborations: The righteous acts are specifically identical with the covenant law kept in all relevant contexts.
The wedding garment in Matthew 22 is directly identical with the fine linen of Revelation 19.
Covenant covering, baptism, foot washing, clean robes, armor, and putting on Christ form one uniform garment system.
A garment is woven through obedience and subsequently washed from the stains introduced by the doer’s sins.
The wedding guest’s lack of a garment means that he had no righteous acts at all.
The breastplate of righteousness and the entire armor of God should be decoded principally through this garment vocabulary.
The helmet of salvation is the Name and word of Jesus covering the mind.
Biblical symbols retain uniform definitions across Scripture whenever sufficiently attested.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The righteous garment primarily symbolizes a divinely bestowed covenantal or forensic acceptance in Christ; obedient deeds are its resulting expression or evidence, but they are not themselves the fundamental basis or fabric of the wearer’s righteous standing.
counter_core_identification: Righteousness in the garment imagery is fundamentally the accepted status God grants through covenant union with Christ, with righteous conduct following from that status.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that performed obedience is what the righteous garment itself principally consists of, treating deeds instead as consequences or signs of a prior granted standing.
counter_case: Isaiah 61:10 presents the robe of righteousness alongside salvation as something with which God clothes the speaker.
The prodigal receives the best robe immediately upon his return, supporting restored acceptance rather than a garment accumulated through prior deeds.
Galatians 3:27 identifies baptismal clothing with putting on Christ, favoring union with Christ as the primary covering.
Zechariah 3:3-5 depicts filthy garments being removed and clean raiment bestowed through God’s removal of iniquity.
Revelation 7:14 says robes are made white in the Lamb’s blood, emphasizing divine cleansing rather than the intrinsic sufficiency of obedience.
Pauline passages such as Romans 4:3-8 and Philippians 3:9 distinguish credited or faith-based righteousness from righteousness grounded in law observance.
book_explanatory_advantages: Deuteronomy 6:25 explicitly calls observing and doing the commandments “our righteousness.”
Psalm 119:172 directly associates all God’s commandments with righteousness.
First John 3:7 grammatically links being righteous with doing righteousness and warns against separating them.
Revelation 19:8 supplies an explicit interpretive key: the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints.
The book preserves both sides of Revelation 19:8: the linen is granted by God, yet the woman actively arrays herself in it.
The conduct reading coherently explains exhortations to put on virtues, avoid defiling garments, keep garments, and bear visible fruit.
It explains why a garment can be worn, soiled, maintained, or absent more concretely than a purely static verdict does.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It better explains passages in which righteousness or righteous clothing is bestowed immediately by God.
It integrates the cleansing power of the Lamb’s blood and the removal of iniquity without making obedience the operative covering.
It handles Pauline forensic language, especially righteousness counted apart from works, more naturally.
It avoids imposing one sense of righteousness on ethical, forensic, divine, covenantal, and christological contexts.
It distinguishes the source of acceptance from the conduct expected of those accepted.
unresolved_objections: The chapter does not adequately reconcile its broad definition with Romans 4:3-8, where righteousness is counted apart from works.
Philippians 3:9 distinguishes righteousness associated with the law from righteousness through faith, complicating any exhaustive equation with law-keeping.
The identification of Matthew 22’s wedding garment with Revelation 19’s fine linen is plausible but not explicitly made by either passage.
The garment’s being granted, the prodigal’s immediate robe, baptismal clothing with Christ, and blood-washed robes may indicate that covenantal acceptance is more fundamental than the chapter allows.
Several symbolic extensions—especially feet as daily conduct, a once-put-on robe as baptism, and the helmet as the Name covering the mind—are suggestive rather than decisively established.
The evidence supports an ethical sense of righteousness in the cited texts but does not prove that righteousness has a single uniform referent throughout Scripture.
Revelation 22:14 has a significant textual variant: many critical editions read “those who wash their robes” rather than “they that do his commandments.”
